fixes.explanation: Close to something a shopkeeper would do, but that's not in the verse. Eliphaz says Job “gave no water” and “withheld food” (Job 22:7). Those are the words he uses for the weary and the famished.
That's a different charge, friend. No town comes up in this verse. For the weary and the famished, Eliphaz says Job gave no water and withheld food (Job 22:7). Water and food are what he names here.
Soldiers never march into this verse, friend. Eliphaz names widows and the fatherless (Job 22:9). He says Job sent widows away empty-handed and the strength of the fatherless was crushed.
Merchants aren't in this verse, friend. Eliphaz says Job sent widows away empty-handed (Job 22:9). He also says the strength of the fatherless was crushed. Those are the two he names.

Correct. Eliphaz claims Job says, “What does God know?” (Job 22:13). He goes on with what he says Job says: “Thick clouds veil Him so He does not see us as He traverses the vault of heaven.” (Job 22:14). Both lines are Eliphaz's claim about Job's words.

That's it. Eliphaz says they told God, “Depart from us. What can the Almighty do to us?” (Job 22:17). Those are the words he gives the wicked men of long ago. He says they were snatched away before their time (Job 22:16).

Right. Eliphaz says, “But it was He who filled their houses with good things…” (Job 22:18). So the good things came from God, in his telling. He says it about the same men who told God, “Depart from us.” (Job 22:17).
Not quite, friend. Eliphaz says the righteous “…see it and are glad…” (Job 22:19). Afraid isn't in the verse. Glad is the word he uses for how they react.
Silent isn't the word in this verse, friend. Eliphaz says, “The righteous see it and are glad…” (Job 22:19). Then he says the innocent mock them. Glad is the one that fits the blank.
